questions.q: Why is ordinary least squares a poor choice for predicting complaints per branch per month?
options: Because a straight line can predict negative counts, and it assumes equal spread when count spread grows with the average
Because least squares cannot use more than one feature
Because counts are categories, so they need logistic regression
Because least squares always predicts whole numbers
questions.why: Counts are never negative and their variance grows with their size; OLS ignores both. Counts are ordered numbers, not yes/no categories, so logistic regression is the wrong family. OLS predictions are not whole numbers either, which is one more mismatch, not a strength.

questions.q: A help desk receives on average **2 calls per minute**, following a Poisson pattern. What is the probability of a minute with **no calls**?
options: 0, because the average is 2
About 0.135
About 0.271
questions.why: P(0) = λ⁰ e^(−λ) / 0! = e^(−2) ≈ 0.135, so about one minute in seven is empty. 0.271 is P(1) = 2e^(−2). An average of 2 does not rule out quiet minutes: the Poisson distribution spreads around its mean.

questions.q: In a footfall model, the coefficient on **heavy_rain (0/1)** is **−0.223**. How should you read it?
options: Rain removes 0.223 visitors per hour
Rain explains 22.3% of the variation in footfall
Rain multiplies expected footfall by e^(−0.223) ≈ 0.80, i.e. about 20% fewer visitors, holding other features fixed
Rain lowers footfall by 0.223%
questions.why: Poisson coefficients live on the log scale, so the effect is the rate ratio e^b, a multiplier on the expected count. Reading the coefficient additively ("0.223 fewer visitors") is the classic mistake the chapter warns about: 0.4 means × 1.49, not +0.4 events.

questions.q: The insurer's model is **log(expected claims per policy-year) = −2.3 + 0.4 × young_driver + 0.1 × (km per year ÷ 10,000)**. What is the expected claim count for a young driver doing **30,000 km** a year, over a full year?
options: About 0.10
About 0.20
About 0.18
questions.why: Score = −2.3 + 0.4 + 0.1 × 3 = −1.6, so the expected count is e^(−1.6) ≈ 0.20 (equivalently 0.100 × 1.49 × e^0.3 ≈ 0.20). −1.6 forgets to exponentiate the score, 0.18 is the chapter's 20,000 km driver, and 0.10 is only the base rate.

questions.q: Branch C has **24 claims over 300 policy-years**; branch D has **40 claims over 800 policy-years**. Which statement is right?
options: D is riskier because it has more claims
They are equally risky because both have tens of claims
C is riskier: 0.08 claims per policy-year against D's 0.05
You cannot compare them without a negative binomial model
questions.why: 24 / 300 = 0.08 and 40 / 800 = 0.05. More exposure naturally produces more claims, which is why Poisson regression uses an exposure offset so the features explain the **rate** per policy-year, not the raw count. Comparing raw counts across windows of different size misleads.

questions.q: A Poisson model of complaints per branch shows a Pearson chi-square / residual degrees of freedom of about **4**. What follows?
options: The model fits perfectly; values above 1 are good
The coefficients are all four times too large and must be divided by 4
There are too many zeros, so the only fix is to drop the zero rows
The data are over-dispersed: standard errors are too small by about √4 = 2, so effects look more significant than they are; consider negative binomial regression
questions.why: Poisson assumes variance = mean; a ratio well above 1 means extra variation. Coefficients stay roughly right, but the standard errors shrink by about √ratio, producing overconfident conclusions. Negative binomial or quasi-Poisson models fix this. Excess zeros are a separate issue handled by zero-inflated or hurdle models, never by deleting data.

questions.q: A plant fits **log(expected defects) = b₀ + b₁ × night**. Day shifts average **3.0** defects and night shifts **4.2**. What is b₁?
options: About 1.099
About 0.336
questions.why: With a single 0/1 feature the Poisson fit matches each group's average, so the rate ratio e^b₁ = 4.2 / 3.0 = 1.4 and b₁ = ln 1.4 ≈ 0.336. 1.4 is the rate ratio itself, not the coefficient; 1.2 is the raw difference in averages (an additive reading); 1.099 is ln 3.0, which is b₀.

questions.q: Interview question: "Why use an **offset** of log(exposure) instead of just adding log(exposure) as an ordinary feature?"
options: An offset fixes the coefficient at 1, forcing expected claims to be exactly proportional to exposure, so the features explain the rate per unit of exposure
There is no difference; an offset is just another name for a feature
Offsets make the model fit faster but give the same coefficients
Offsets are only needed when the data are over-dispersed
questions.why: log μ = log(exposure) + b₀ + … means μ = exposure × rate: twice the policy-years, twice the expected claims. As a free feature, the model could estimate any coefficient on log(exposure) and blur the line between "more exposure" and "higher risk". Offsets are about unequal observation windows, not over-dispersion.
